summary: For 6-7 year olds, help children plan a pathway through two-step and more complex word problems: identify what is known and what must be found, decide which information is relevant (setting aside any red-herring number), choose and sequence operations, estimate first, and check the answer for reasonableness. Two documented habits work against this: keyword/number-grabbing (choosing an operation from a cue word or using every number present) and the compulsion to calculate (rushing to an answer with no estimate or sense-check). The strongest supports in the sources are teacher-modelled self-questioning and children building their OWN visual representations (strip/bar diagrams, or a number line for two-step jumps) that map relevant quantities and reveal the sequence of steps. Several activities below address the same objective through different media (a build-your-own workspace, a planning dialogue, a worked-example companion, and a reasonableness-judgement item); keep more than one because they exercise construction, talk, and recognition respectively.
misconceptions: Answering only the first step of a two-step problem (treating multi-step as single-step)
Using every number in the problem, including an irrelevant one, because 'they must all be needed'
Choosing the operation from a cue word rather than the problem's structure
Computing an answer and stopping, with no estimate or reasonableness check (compulsion to calculate)

activities.title: Build-your-own 'plan-it' workspace with a red herring and an estimate-first step
steps: Meet a problem revealed a piece at a time: first the story, then the question, then the numbers (a staged, numberless-to-numbered reveal).
Build your OWN representation by dragging parts onto a canvas to map the known parts to the unknown — a bar/strip diagram, or a number line to show the jumps — rather than using a pre-made diagram.

Identify and physically set aside the irrelevant number. For example, in 'There are 24 children and 3 teachers; 8 children go home. How many children are left?' the 3 teachers are not needed (this one is a single step, 24 − 8 = 16, chosen to practise spotting a red herring).

Practise the sequencing on a genuinely two-step version, e.g. '8 children go home in the morning and 6 more go home at lunch; how many are left?' — here finding 16 is only step one (24 − 8), and 10 is the answer (16 − 6).
Before computing, set an estimate ('about how big will the answer be?') to create a reasonableness benchmark.

Compute, then compare the answer to your own estimate; when the answer lands far from the estimate, re-check — did you stop after step one, use the spare number, or (in problems where order matters) do the steps in the wrong order?
Return to the still-visible model to complete or fix the second step.
activities.insight: Planning, relevance-sorting, and self-checking become things the child does and watches on a live representation, rather than rules they are told. Keeping the whole situation visible helps the child notice when they have stopped after step one on multi-step problems, and comparing to a self-made estimate can make an unreasonable answer stand out.

activities.title: Planning dialogue with a 'detective partner' that models self-questioning
steps: Work with an in-role partner who models self-questioning aloud and asks you to answer: 'What do I know? What must I find? What shall I do first? Does that make sense?'
Say which information is needed and which is a red herring, and justify your plan aloud before computing.
Before computing, estimate ('about how big should the answer be?'), then close every problem by sense-checking the result against that estimate.
When your first approach stalls, try 'let's show it another way' — represent the problem differently (for example, swap a bar model for a number line) rather than abandoning it.
activities.insight: Rehearsing the monitoring routine in talk — planning the pathway, naming relevant versus irrelevant information, and sense-checking — builds the habit of reasoning about structure before numbers.

activities.title: Worked-example companion: reveal a good solver's self-questions and why a number was ignored
steps: Work through a tap-to-reveal worked two-step problem, uncovering each phase: understand → plan → solve → check.
At each phase, reveal the self-question a good solver asks and why the irrelevant number was ignored.
After viewing, retell the plan in your own words and then try a fresh problem where YOU do the planning and relevance-sorting.
activities.insight: Seeing the plan-then-check frame and the reasoning for discarding a spare number makes the usually-invisible monitoring moves explicit before the child performs them independently.

activities.title: 'Which answer is unreasonable, and why?' judgement item
steps: Read a 'take away' story and an offered answer that is larger than the starting amount.
Decide whether the answer is reasonable, and explain WHY using the situation (e.g. 'fewer than 24 should be left because some children went home').
Where possible, state roughly how big the answer should be before judging it.
activities.insight: Judging reasonableness against the situation — not re-computing — rehearses the estimate-and-sense-check habit and can surface the compulsion-to-calculate pattern.

activities.title: Replace keyword cues with problem-structure reasoning
steps: Retell a word problem in your own words before touching any numbers.
Decide the operation from the problem's structure (part-part-whole, comparison/'more than', two-step change), not from a cue word.
Map the relevant quantities onto a part-part-whole or comparison bar so the structure, not a keyword, drives the plan.
Test a trap problem where a 'more than' phrase does not mean 'add', to see that keywords are unreliable.
activities.insight: Keywords are not tied to one operation; reasoning from the problem's structure (schema) is more reliable than grabbing an operation from a cue word.

checkQuestion: Give a two-step problem within 100 that contains one irrelevant number, e.g. 'There are 24 children and 3 teachers. 8 children go home. How many children are left?' Before any answer ask: 'How do you decide what to do first? Which numbers do you actually need? Show me your plan.' Then: 'About how big should the answer be — and once you have it, how would you know it makes sense?' Discuss the thinking; do not mark the number right or wrong.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who identifies the relevant numbers (24 and 8) and sets aside the 3 teachers as not needed, plans a pathway (start with 24, take away 8), estimates it will be 'a bit less than 24', gets 16, and checks it makes sense (fewer than 24 because some went home). The planning, relevance-sorting and reasonableness talk are the targets, not the subtraction itself.
